title: Constructions
tagline: Ruler and compass constructions of standard geometric figures, with fully justified steps.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Constructions are geometric drawings performed using only a ruler (without measurement markings) and a compass. In ICSE Class X Mathematics, students are expected to perform standard constructions and, crucially, state the geometric justification for each step. This chapter covers the six constructions prescribed by the ICSE syllabus: bisecting a given angle, drawing the perpendicular bisector of a given segment, constructing a line perpendicular to a given line through a given point (on the line and off the line), constructing an angle equal to a given angle, and constructing a triangle given certain conditions. Each construction is presented with clearly numbered steps and a written justification.

facts.label: Ruler (no markings)
facts.value: Used only to draw straight lines through existing points; never to measure lengths.

facts.label: Compass
facts.value: Used to transfer distances and draw arcs/circles; the pencil must not be lifted during a construction step.

facts.label: Perpendicular bisector
facts.value: The line that is perpendicular to a segment and passes through its midpoint.

facts.label: Angle bisector
facts.value: The ray that divides an angle into two equal angles.

facts.label: Construction vs. drawing
facts.value: A construction is justified by geometric reasoning; a drawing may be approximate.

learningOutcomes: Perform each of the six prescribed constructions with ruler and compass.
State the geometric justification for every construction step.
Distinguish between the construction steps and the justification.
Construct a triangle given: (i) base, one base angle, and the sum of the other two sides, (ii) base, one base angle, and the difference of the other two sides, (iii) the three side lengths (SSS).
Verify a construction by measuring or by checking that the stated conditions are satisfied.
Explain why a ruler without markings and a compass are the only permitted tools.

blocks.text: In geometric constructions, we use two tools only: an unmarked ruler (to draw straight lines) and a compass (to draw arcs and circles and to transfer distances). The pencil must remain on the paper during each step — lifting the pencil invalidates the construction. Every construction must be justified: that is, you must give a geometric reason (such as 'triangle congruence', 'properties of isosceles triangles', 'perpendicular bisector theorem', etc.) for why each step works. Constructions are not 'drawings'; they are logically derived positions that must satisfy the stated conditions.
A blank workspace showing the six construction types with space for step-by-step drawings.

items: Only an unmarked ruler and a compass may be used.
The pencil must not be lifted from the paper during a construction step.
Each step must be justified by a geometric reason.
After completing a construction, verify that it satisfies the required condition.
Constructions are assessed on correctness of steps and quality of justifications.

blocks.text: Construction: To bisect a given angle ∠ABC (with vertex B).

steps.text: With centre B, draw a circle of any radius, cutting the arms BA and BC at points E and F respectively.
With centres E and F and the same radius (greater than half EF), draw two circles intersecting at point G (take the intersection inside the angle).
Draw the ray BG. This ray is the bisector of ∠ABC.

justification.text: Step 1: Circle centred at B gives BE = BF (radii of the same circle).
Step 2: Circles centred at E and F with equal radii give EG = FG (intersecting circles have equal radii from centres to the intersection point). Also, BE = BF (from step 1).
Step 3: In triangles BEG and BF EG, we have BE = BF, EG = FG, and BG is common. By SSS congruence, ∠EBG = ∠FBG. Hence BG bisects ∠ABC.

items: The compass radius in step 2 must be greater than half the distance EF for the circles to intersect.
The intersection point G must be chosen inside the angle (not outside).
The justification uses SSS congruence: BE = BF, EG = FG, BG common → ∠EBG = ∠FBG.
Always label the intersection points clearly in your diagram.

learn.title: Construction 2: Perpendicular Bisector of a Given Segment

blocks.text: Construction: To draw the perpendicular bisector of a given line segment AB.

steps.text: With centre A and radius greater than half AB, draw a circle.
With centre B and the same radius, draw another circle, intersecting the first circle at points C and D.
Draw the line CD. This line is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

justification.text: Step 1: Circle centred at A gives that all points at that radius from A are on the circle.
Circle centred at B with the same radius gives that C and D are equidistant from A and B: AC = BC and AD = BD.

Step 3: In triangles ACD and BCD, we have AC = BC, AD = BD, and CD is common. By SSS congruence, ∠ACD = ∠BCD and ∠ADC = ∠BDC. Since CD makes adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°, each of ∠ACD and ∠BCD is 90°. Hence CD ⟂ AB and M (the intersection of CD and AB) is the midpoint of AB.

items: The compass radius must be greater than half AB for the two circles to intersect at two points.
The line CD is the perpendicular bisector: it is perpendicular to AB and passes through the midpoint.
The justification uses SSS congruence: AC = BC, AD = BD, CD common.
The point where CD meets AB is the midpoint of AB.

learn.title: Construction 3: Perpendicular to a Given Line Through a Point

blocks.text: Case A: The point lies on the given line.
Construction: To draw a line perpendicular to a given line l through a point P on l.

steps.text: With centre P, draw a circle of any radius, cutting line l at points Q and R.
With centres Q and R and the same radius (greater than QR), draw two circles intersecting at point S (take the intersection on the opposite side of l from P).
Draw the line PS. This line is perpendicular to l.

justification.text: Step 1: Circle centred at P gives PQ = PR (radii of the same circle).
Step 2: Circles centred at Q and R with equal radii give QS = RS (intersecting circles). Also, PQ = PR (from step 1).
Step 3: In triangles PQS and PRS, we have PQ = PR, QS = RS, and PS is common. By SSS congruence, ∠QPS = ∠RPS. Since ∠QPS and ∠RPS form a linear pair, each is 90°. Hence PS ⟂ l.

items: The two intersection points Q and R must be on opposite sides of P on line l.
The radius in step 2 must be large enough for the circles to intersect.
The justification uses SSS congruence: PQ = PR, QS = RS, PS common → ∠QPS = ∠RPS = 90°.

blocks.text: Case B: The point does not lie on the given line.
Construction: To draw a line perpendicular to a given line l through a point P not on l.

steps.text: From P, draw a circle cutting line l at two points A and B (the circle must intersect l in two points).
Construct the perpendicular bisector of segment AB (using Construction 2). Let the bisector meet l at point Q.
Draw the line PQ. This line is perpendicular to l.

justification.text: Step 1: Circle centred at P intersects l at A and B, giving PA = PB (radii of the same circle).

Step 2: The perpendicular bisector of AB is constructed (Construction 2), so it is perpendicular to AB and passes through the midpoint of AB. Since A and B lie on l, the bisector is also perpendicular to l.
Step 3: The line PQ is the same as the perpendicular bisector of AB (since Q is the intersection of the bisector with l), so PQ ⟂ l.

items: The circle in step 1 must be large enough to intersect line l in two points.
Construction 2 (perpendicular bisector) is used as a sub-step.
The justification chains: circle → PA = PB → perp bisector of AB → perpendicular to l.

learn.title: Construction 4: Construct an Angle Equal to a Given Angle

blocks.text: Construction: To construct an angle at point P on line l that is equal to a given angle ∠ABC.

steps.text: With centre B, draw a circle of any radius, cutting the arms BA and BC at points E and F respectively.
With centre P and the same radius, draw a circle cutting line l at point Q.
With centre Q and radius equal to EF, draw a circle cutting the circle from step 2 at point R.
Draw the ray PR. The angle ∠RPQ is equal to ∠ABC.

justification.text: Step 1: Circle centred at B gives BE = BF (radii of the same circle).
Step 2: Circle centred at P with the same radius gives PQ = BE = BF (all radii of circles with equal radii).
Step 3: Circle centred at Q with radius EF gives QR = EF. Also, the arc from step 1 gives chord EF, and the arc from step 3 gives chord QR equal to EF.
Step 4: In triangles BEF and PQR, we have BE = PQ, BF = PR (radii of equal circles), and EF = QR (by construction). By SSS congruence, ∠EBF = ∠RPQ. Hence ∠RPQ = ∠ABC.

items: The radius in step 1 must be chosen so that the circle cuts both arms of the given angle.
The radius in step 3 must equal the chord EF from step 1, not the radius itself.
The justification uses SSS congruence: BE = PQ, BF = PR, EF = QR → ∠EBF = ∠RPQ.
After construction, verify that the new angle measures the same as the given angle using a protractor (for verification only; constructions are not assessed by measurement).

learn.title: Construction 5: Construct a Triangle Given Base, One Base Angle, and Sum of the Other Two Sides

blocks.text: Construction: To construct triangle ABC given base BC, base angle ∠B, and the sum AB + AC.

steps.text: Draw the base BC.
At point B, construct the given angle ∠CBX (ray BX on one side of BC).
On ray BX, mark point D such that BD = AB + AC (any convenient length, then adjust).
Join D to C.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of DC, meeting ray BX at point A.
Join A to C. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

justification.text: Step 1: Drawing the base BC gives the fixed side.
Step 2: Constructing ∠CBX at B gives the fixed base angle.
Step 3: Marking BD = AB + AC on the ray ensures that the total length from B to D equals the given sum.
Step 5: A lies on the perpendicular bisector of DC, so AD = AC (property of perpendicular bisector). Since BD = AB + AC, we have AB = BD − AD = BD − AC, which gives AB + AC = BD, the given sum.
Step 6: Triangle ABC is formed with base BC, base angle ∠B (since A lies on ray BX), and AB + AC = BD (the given sum).

items: The length BD in step 3 must be set to the given sum AB + AC. In practice, any convenient length can be used, and the construction adjusts via the perpendicular bisector.
The perpendicular bisector of DC is key: any point on it is equidistant from D and C.
The justification chains: A on perp bisector of DC → AD = AC → AB = BD − AC → AB + AC = BD.
This construction works only if the given sum AB + AC > BC (triangle inequality).

learn.title: Construction 6: Construct a Triangle Given Base, One Base Angle, and Difference of the Other Two Sides

blocks.text: Case 1: AB > AC (the difference AB − AC is given).
Construction: To construct triangle ABC given base BC, base angle ∠B, and the difference AB − AC.

steps.text: Draw the base BC.
At point B, construct the given angle ∠CBX (ray BX on one side of BC).
On ray BX, mark point D such that BD = AB − AC (mark the difference length from B towards X).
Join D to C.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of DC, meeting ray BX at point A (on the side of D towards X).
Join A to C. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

justification.text: Step 1: Drawing the base BC gives the fixed side.
Step 2: Constructing ∠CBX at B gives the fixed base angle.
Step 3: Marking BD = AB − AC on the ray ensures that the length from B to D equals the given difference.
Step 5: A lies on the perpendicular bisector of DC, so AD = AC. Since BD = AB − AC, we have AB = BD + AD = BD + AC, which gives AB − AC = BD, the given difference.
Step 6: Triangle ABC is formed with base BC, base angle ∠B, and AB − AC = BD (the given difference).

items: The length BD in step 3 must be set to the given difference AB − AC.
The perpendicular bisector of DC ensures AD = AC.
The justification chains: A on perp bisector of DC → AD = AC → AB = BD + AC → AB − AC = BD.
This construction works only if the given difference satisfies the triangle inequality: AB − AC < BC < AB + AC.

blocks.text: Case 2: AC > AB (the difference AC − AB is given).
Construction: To construct triangle ABC given base BC, base angle ∠B, and the difference AC − AB.

steps.text: Draw the base BC.
At point B, construct the given angle ∠CBX (ray BX on one side of BC).
Extend XB backwards through B to the opposite side of BC, and on this extension mark point D such that BD = AC − AB.
Join DC.
Draw the perpendicular bisector of DC. Let it meet ray BX at A.
Join AC. Triangle ABC is the required triangle (A lies on the perpendicular bisector of DC, so AD = AC, and AD = AB + BD gives AC − AB = BD).

keyPoints: Use only an unmarked straightedge for drawing straight lines and a compass for arcs and transferring distances; measurement with scale markings or a protractor is not part of a construction.
Keep the compass radius fixed within a step where equality of lengths is required, because equal radii create the congruent segments used in justifications.
The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the locus of points equidistant from its endpoints and can be constructed by arcs of equal radius from each endpoint.
The bisector of an angle is constructed by equal arcs on the arms and intersecting arcs from those points, giving equal distances needed for congruent triangles.

A perpendicular to a line at a point on it is constructed using equal intercepts on the line and intersecting arcs; from a point outside, use equal distances to cut the line and then bisect the chord.
To copy an angle, transfer one arc to set corresponding points on the arms and transfer the chord length between those points to fix the opening.

To construct a triangle given base, a base angle and the sum of the other two sides, mark the sum on the arm of the given angle and use the perpendicular bisector to locate the third vertex so that two sides differ by the required amount.

To construct a triangle given base, a base angle and the difference of the other two sides, mark the difference on the appropriate side of the base angle ray and use the perpendicular bisector of the joining segment.
Every construction must be accompanied by clear steps and a geometric justification, commonly using congruence (SSS, SAS) or properties of perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors.
Neat labelling, visible construction arcs and verification against given data (lengths, angle, sum or difference) are essential for a correct and complete construction.
examFocus: Write construction steps in order and include brief justifications; marks are often awarded for both procedure and reasoning.
State the compass radius condition clearly where needed, such as taking radius greater than half the segment for intersecting arcs.
Do not erase construction arcs; they show the method and support the justification.
When constructing perpendicular bisectors or angle bisectors, name the congruent triangles or equal distances used to prove the result.

For triangle constructions with sum or difference of sides, draw a clear rough sketch mentally, mark the given base angle correctly, and justify the location of the third vertex using the perpendicular bisector property.
Label all points in the same order as stated in the question and verify the final figure satisfies the given measurements or conditions.
Use sharp pencil and accurate arcs; small drafting errors can make verification fail even when steps are known.
Distinguish between drawing (measurement-based) and construction (compass-and-straightedge with proof); exam questions expect construction.

vocabulary.meaning: An unmarked ruler used only to draw straight lines joining points.
An instrument used to draw arcs/circles and transfer equal lengths.
A part of the circumference of a circle drawn with a compass.
The set of all points satisfying a given geometric condition.
A line perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint; every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints.
A ray dividing an angle into two equal angles; points on it are equidistant from the arms (within the angle).
Triangles equal in shape and size, used to justify equal angles or sides in constructions.
If three sides of one triangle equal three sides of another, the triangles are congruent.
The point where two lines or arcs meet, often determining a required vertex or line.
An angle at an endpoint of the base of a triangle.
Checking the completed figure against given lengths, angles or conditions.
The geometric reasoning explaining why construction steps produce the required figure.

Marks indicate AM = MB and PA = PB = QA = QB, showing equal radii and the midpoint.

Ray BF is drawn from B through F, dividing angle ABC into two equal angles. Tick marks on BD and BE, and on DF and EF, indicate equal compass lengths.

figures.description: Base BC is drawn as a segment. At B a ray BX makes the given base angle with BC. Point D is marked on BX so that BD equals AB + AC. Segment DC is joined and its perpendicular bisector is constructed, meeting BX at A. Triangle ABC is completed by joining A to C. A dashed indication shows AD = AC by the perpendicular bisector property, hence AB + AC = BD.

questions.prompt: Which instruments are permitted for a standard geometric construction in this chapter?
options: An unmarked straightedge and a compass
A protractor and a marked ruler
A set square and a divider only
A marked ruler and a protractor only
questions.answer: An unmarked straightedge and a compass
questions.explanation: Standard ruler-and-compass constructions use an unmarked straightedge to draw lines and a compass to draw arcs and transfer lengths; measuring instruments like protractors or marked scales are not used for the construction steps.

questions.prompt: To construct the perpendicular bisector of segment AB, arcs are drawn from A and B with radius:
options: less than half of AB
greater than half of AB
exactly equal to AB only
equal to one quarter of AB
questions.answer: greater than half of AB
questions.explanation: The radius must be greater than half of AB so that the arcs from centres A and B intersect at two points on opposite sides of AB; a smaller radius would not produce intersections.

questions.prompt: In bisecting angle ABC, arcs of equal radius from points on BA and BC intersect at G. Ray BG bisects the angle because:
options: BG is the longest segment in the figure
triangles formed are similar but not congruent
triangles BEG and BFG are congruent by SSS
point G is always the midpoint of AC
questions.answer: triangles BEG and BFG are congruent by SSS
questions.explanation: BE = BF (radii from B), EG = FG (equal radii from E and F), and BG is common, so triangles BEG and BFG are congruent by SSS, giving ∠EBG = ∠FBG.

questions.prompt: When copying angle ABC at point P on a line, after drawing equal arcs from B and P, the next compass setting should be:
options: the radius of the first arc again
half the distance between B and C
any convenient length greater than BC
the distance between the arc intersections on BA and BC
questions.answer: the distance between the arc intersections on BA and BC
questions.explanation: Transferring the chord length between the points where the first arc cuts the arms of angle ABC ensures the copied angle has the same opening, justified by SSS congruence.

questions.prompt: The perpendicular bisector of a line segment is the locus of points that are:
options: equidistant from the two endpoints of the segment
equidistant from the two arms of an angle
at a fixed distance from one endpoint only
closest to the midpoint but not equidistant
questions.answer: equidistant from the two endpoints of the segment
questions.explanation: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equidistant from A and B, and conversely any point equidistant from A and B lies on this bisector.

questions.prompt: In constructing a triangle given base BC, angle at B, and AB + AC, point D is marked on the ray at B so that BD equals AB + AC. Vertex A is located by constructing:
options: the angle bisector of angle BDC
the perpendicular bisector of DC
a perpendicular from C to BD
the midpoint of BC only
questions.answer: the perpendicular bisector of DC
questions.explanation: Any point A on the perpendicular bisector of DC satisfies AD = AC. Since BD = AB + AD = AB + AC, choosing A as the intersection of this bisector with the ray gives the required triangle.

questions.prompt: A triangle with base BC = 6 cm, angle B = 60°, and AB − AC = 2 cm (with AB > AC) can be constructed because:
options: the difference of two sides may be greater than the third side
the sum of all three sides is given directly
AB − AC < BC and the given data satisfy triangle conditions
AB + AC must equal BC in this case
questions.answer: AB − AC < BC and the given data satisfy triangle conditions
questions.explanation: For a triangle, |AB − AC| must be less than BC. Here 2 cm < 6 cm, so the data are consistent and the standard construction (marking the difference on the ray of the base angle and using a perpendicular bisector) is possible.

questions.prompt: To construct a perpendicular to line l from a point P not on l, the first step is to:
options: draw any line through P parallel to l
measure the distance from P to l with a ruler
draw the perpendicular bisector of l without using P
draw an arc with centre P cutting l at two points
questions.answer: draw an arc with centre P cutting l at two points
questions.explanation: An arc centred at P that cuts line l at two points A and B gives PA = PB. The perpendicular bisector (or equivalent arc construction) of AB then passes through P and is perpendicular to l.

questions.prompt: A line that divides a given angle into two equal angles is called the ______ of the angle.
questions.answer: bisector
questions.explanation: The angle bisector is the ray from the vertex that splits the angle into two congruent angles.

questions.prompt: The perpendicular bisector of a segment passes through its ______.
questions.answer: midpoint
questions.explanation: By definition, a perpendicular bisector is perpendicular to the segment and divides it into two equal parts at its midpoint.

questions.prompt: In ruler-and-compass constructions, arcs of equal radius are used to create equal ______ needed for justification.
questions.answer: lengths
questions.explanation: Equal compass openings produce equal radii, giving equal line segments that are used to prove congruence or locus properties in the justification.

questions.prompt: State the two tools allowed in geometric constructions and the purpose of each.
questions.answer: An unmarked straightedge is used to draw straight lines through given points. A compass is used to draw arcs/circles and to transfer equal lengths.
questions.explanation: Constructions rely on creating equal distances and straight joins without measurement markings, so only these two tools are permitted.

questions.prompt: Why must the radius be greater than half of AB when constructing the perpendicular bisector of AB?
questions.answer: If the radius is greater than half of AB, the arcs from A and B intersect at two points; if it is equal to or less than half, the arcs will not intersect in two points and the bisector cannot be drawn.
questions.explanation: Two circles (or arcs) intersect in two points only when the distance between centres is less than the sum of radii and greater than the difference, which here requires radius > AB/2 for equal radii.

questions.prompt: In the construction to copy an angle, which lengths are made equal to justify that the constructed angle equals the given angle?
questions.answer: The radii from the vertices are equal (giving corresponding sides on the arms equal) and the chord distance between the arc-arm intersection points is transferred as equal, so the two triangles formed are congruent by SSS and the included angles are equal.
questions.explanation: Copying the opening requires three pairs of equal sides in the triangles determined by the vertex, one arc point on each arm, and the chord joining those arc points.

questions.prompt: Give the key property used to locate the third vertex when constructing a triangle given base BC, angle B and sum AB + AC.
questions.answer: Point A is taken on the perpendicular bisector of DC (where BD = AB + AC on the ray of angle B), so AD = AC. Therefore AB = BD − AD = BD − AC, giving AB + AC = BD as required.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector locus provides equidistance AD = AC, converting the sum condition into a measurable length BD on a known ray.

questions.prompt: Describe the steps to construct the perpendicular bisector of a given line segment AB and justify why the line obtained is perpendicular to AB and bisects it.
questions.answer: Steps: (1) With centre A and radius greater than half AB, draw arcs above and below AB. (2) With centre B and the same radius, draw arcs intersecting the previous arcs at P and Q. (3) Join PQ to meet AB at M. Justification: PA = PB and QA = QB (equal radii). In triangles PAQ and PBQ, PA = PB, QA = QB and PQ is common, so ΔPAQ ≅ ΔPBQ (SSS) and ∠APQ = ∠BPQ. In triangles APM and BPM, PA = PB, PM common and included angles equal, so ΔAPM ≅ ΔBPM (SAS). Hence AM = MB and ∠AMP = ∠BMP = 90°, so PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB.
questions.explanation: The construction uses equal radii to create congruent triangles; SAS congruence gives both equality of halves (midpoint) and right angles (perpendicularity).

questions.prompt: Explain how to construct a triangle ABC given BC = 7 cm, ∠B = 60° and AB + AC = 10 cm. Include the main justification.
questions.answer: Steps: (1) Draw BC = 7 cm. (2) At B construct ∠CBX = 60°. (3) On BX mark D such that BD = 10 cm. (4) Join DC. (5) Construct the perpendicular bisector of DC to meet BX at A. (6) Join AC. Triangle ABC is required. Justification: A lies on the perpendicular bisector of DC, so AD = AC. Thus AB + AC = AB + AD = BD = 10 cm, and ∠B and base BC are as given.
questions.explanation: The condition on the sum of two sides is converted into a fixed length BD on the ray of the given angle; equidistance from the perpendicular bisector ensures AD = AC.

questions.prompt: Explain how to construct a triangle ABC given BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 45° and AB − AC = 2 cm (AB > AC). State the essential justification.
questions.answer: Steps: (1) Draw BC = 6 cm. (2) At B construct ∠CBX = 45°. (3) On ray BX mark D such that BD = 2 cm. (4) Join DC. (5) Construct the perpendicular bisector of DC to meet BX produced beyond D at A. (6) Join AC. Triangle ABC is required. Justification: A lies on the perpendicular bisector of DC, so AD = AC. Since A is beyond D on BX, AB = AD + DB = AC + 2 cm, hence AB − AC = 2 cm with base BC and ∠B as given.
questions.explanation: For AB > AC the difference is marked along the base-angle ray from B toward X; the perpendicular bisector of DC locates A so that AD = AC and the difference condition holds.

questions.prompt: A student draws arcs of radius 2 cm from ends of a segment AB of length 6 cm to construct its perpendicular bisector, but the arcs do not intersect. Analyse the error and state the correct condition with reasoning.
questions.answer: The error is choosing radius 2 cm, which is not greater than half of AB (half of 6 cm is 3 cm). With centres 6 cm apart and equal radii 2 cm, the circles do not meet because 2 + 2 < 6. The correct condition is radius r > AB/2 (for equal radii), for example r = 4 cm, so that arcs intersect at two points and the line joining them is the perpendicular bisector.
questions.explanation: Intersection of two circles requires the sum of radii to exceed the distance between centres (and difference conditions satisfied); using a radius ≤ half the segment violates this and prevents the construction.

questions.prompt: While constructing an angle equal to a given angle, a student transfers the first arc radius correctly but takes a different compass opening (not equal to the chord EF) in the next step. Analyse what goes wrong and identify the correct equalities needed.
questions.answer: If the second opening is not equal to chord EF, the point R obtained will not make QR = EF, so triangles BEF and PQR will not satisfy SSS congruence and ∠RPQ will not equal ∠EBF. The correct construction requires BE = PQ, BF = PR (same arc radius) and EF = QR (transferred chord length), ensuring ΔBEF ≅ ΔPQR and equality of the angles at B and P.
questions.explanation: Copying an angle depends on reproducing the triangle formed by two radii and the included chord; changing the chord length alters the included angle.

questions.prompt: For constructing triangle ABC with base BC, angle B, and difference of the other two sides given as AC − AB (with AC > AB), a student marks the difference on ray BX as in the AB > AC case and cannot locate A correctly. Analyse the mistake and describe the correct placement.
questions.answer: When AC > AB, point D must be marked on the extension of XB backwards through B (on the side opposite to ray BX) such that BD = AC − AB. Marking D on BX gives the AB > AC configuration. With D correctly placed opposite, joining DC and constructing its perpendicular bisector to meet ray BX at A gives AD = AC and AD = AB + BD, hence AC − AB = BD as required.
questions.explanation: The direction of BD relative to B determines whether AD adds to or subtracts from AB along the ray; reversing the case requires reversing the side on which the difference is marked.

questions.prompt: After constructing the perpendicular bisector of AB, a student claims it is correct because it 'looks perpendicular'. Evaluate this claim and state a geometric justification that should accompany the construction.
questions.answer: Visual appearance is not a proof. The construction is justified because arcs of equal radius give PA = PB and QA = QB; with PQ common, triangles PAQ and PBQ are congruent (SSS), leading to congruent adjacent triangles at M and hence AM = MB and ∠AMP = ∠BMP = 90°. The line is the perpendicular bisector because it satisfies both midpoint and perpendicularity by congruence, not by appearance.
questions.explanation: Constructions require logical justification from equal lengths and congruence; measurement or visual judgement cannot replace geometric reasoning.
